what: This is the control for the Obliquity Orrery. Every part, the orbit and the motor program are the same, except that the angle connector under the Earth is turned 90° about its vertical spindle, and the Sun marker is left out because the turned Earth would hit it. The Earth's axis is still tilted by 22.5° and still keeps its direction, but it now leans in a different horizontal direction. The declination is measured against the same orbit-centre point. In the simulator midsummer moves from λ = 45° to λ = 135°, and δ follows sin δ = sin 22.5° · cos(λ − 135°) within 0.01°.
try: Load this control, press Reset, then Run, and watch the Earth's axis. It still keeps one direction, but it now leans along the orbit at the start instead of towards the Sun.

Compare the two runs station by station. In the main model δ falls from 22.5° to 0° over the sweep. In this control the Earth starts at λ = 112.5° with δ = 20.7°, reaches midsummer (22.5°) halfway, at λ = 135°, and ends at λ = 157.5° with δ = 20.7° again.
Use the manual jog on port A to step the orbit in 15° steps and estimate the axis lean towards the orbit centre at each step in both models.

Note that the Earth here sits on a slightly smaller circle round the Sun point (12.2 mm instead of 16 mm), because the Earth is mounted off the spindle. The declination does not depend on that radius.
why: The declination only depends on the axis direction n and the direction s to the Sun: sin δ = n · s. Turning the connector turns the horizontal part of n, sin ε, to a new azimuth, while its vertical part cos ε stays the same. The cosine law keeps its shape but shifts: sin δ = sin ε · cos(λ − λ₀) with λ₀ = 135° here instead of 45°. So the tilt angle decides how large the seasons are, and the direction of the tilt decides when in the orbit they happen. A causal control has to change exactly one thing and predict a different result: here the prediction is the 90° shift, and the measured sequence of declinations shifts by 90°.
matters: The direction of the Earth's tilt is not fixed for ever: the axis slowly circles round, once in about 26,000 years (precession). In about 13,000 years the northern summer will fall at the point of the orbit where the northern winter is today. Together with slow changes in the tilt and the orbit's shape, this shifts the seasons against the orbit and paces the ice ages (the Milankovitch cycles).
question: This Earth ends the sweep at λ = 157.5°. What declination does the formula predict there, and what does the main model show at the end of its sweep?
answer: sin δ = sin 22.5° · cos(157.5° − 135°) = 0.383 · 0.924 = 0.354, so δ = 20.7°, close to midsummer. The main model ends at its equinox, δ = 0°. Same tilt, same motor program: only the direction of the tilt differs, and it moves the seasons a quarter of an orbit along.
further: Predict where midsummer would fall if the connector were turned 180°. Why is that version not shipped? (Its Earth would hit the frame.)
Precession turns the real Earth's axis by about 50 arc seconds per year. How many years does it take to move the solstice by one day of the orbit?
Which result in the two runs would show that the coupler really does not rotate?
formula: sin δ = sin ε · cos(λ − 135°), ε = 22.5°; sin δ = n · s; λ = direction of the Earth from the orbit-centre point; orbit radius here 12.2 mm.
